function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to help you set up the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub‑Actions workflow for the **nodejs‑welcome** project, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone repositories, run commands locally, or push commits back to GitHub.  
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow on your own machine, along with the code snippets that the helper functions will generate for you.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Artifacts

### 2.1 Create/Update the Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a typical Node.js application (e.g., an `app.js` or `server.js` entry point), we’ll generate a minimal Dockerfile that uses the official Node.js slim image.

```bash
# Run this from the root of the cloned repo
python - <<'PY'
from functions import create_a_docker_file
create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",          # Current directory
    base_image="node:18-slim",   # Use a recent Node.js LTS image
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,            # Adjust if your app listens elsewhere
    entrypoint="node app.js"     # Change to your actual entry point
)
PY
```

> **What the function does:**  
> * Creates a `Dockerfile` in the specified directory (`.`).  
> * Uses the chosen base image (`node:18-slim`).  
> * Sets the maintainer label.  
> * Exposes port `3000`.  
> * Sets the default command to `node app.js`.

If you prefer to edit the Dockerfile manually, here’s a template you can copy:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-slim

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose port
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Adjustments you might need:**
> * Replace `app.js` with whatever your main script is called.
> * If you use Yarn, change `npm ci` to `yarn install --production`.
> * Add environment variables or health‑check instructions as needed.

---

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Let’s create a Deployment and Service that expose the Node.js app inside a cluster.

```bash
python - <<'PY'
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file
create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name=".",              # Root of the repo
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome",
    image_name="your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=3,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
PY
```

> **What the function does:**  
> * Writes a `kubernetes.yaml` file containing both a Deployment and a Service.  
> * Uses the image name you provide (replace with your actual registry/tag).  
> * Deploys 3 replicas listening on port 3000.  
> * Exposes the Service as a `ClusterIP` (internal only).

If you’d like to edit the YAML manually, here’s a ready‑to‑copy template:

```yaml
# kubernetes.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Customizations:**
> * Change `replicas` to suit your scaling needs.
> * Switch `service_type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you want external access.
> * Add resource limits, liveness/readiness probes, or environment variables as required.

---

### 2.3 Create a GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a `.github/workflows/ci.yml` file that builds the Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub whenever you push to `main`.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Setup required:**
> 1. In your GitHub repo settings → Secrets → Actions, add:
>    * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.
>    * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password).
> 2. Replace `your-dockerhub-username` with your actual Docker Hub account name.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the New Files

```bash
git add Dockerfile kubernetes.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Result:**  
> * Your repo now contains a Dockerfile, a Kubernetes deployment/service manifest, and a GitHub Actions workflow that automatically builds and pushes the image on each push to `main`.

---

### Recap of What I Can Do for You

| Task | What I can provide |
|------|--------------------|
| Generate Dockerfile | `create_a_docker_file` function |
| Generate Kubernetes YAML | `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` function |
| Provide CI workflow template | Manual YAML snippet |
